claims.claim: Kay says the quarter turn means even a reader who knows the real history cannot be sure where the novel is going.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History' (first published at boingboing.net, 2016), Bright Weavings
claims.quote: he or she cannot be sure they know where the novel
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'I had come to realize'

claims.claim: Kay says he telescoped the Reconquista in The Lions of Al-Rassan so a culture's demise plays out in one or two generations.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History' (first published at boingboing.net, 2016), Bright Weavings
claims.quote: I telescoped the Reconquista in Lions
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'It was with Lions'

claims.claim: Kay says the Sarantine Mosaic let him develop thoughts about Procopius the historian and about the writers of history and chroniclers.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History' (first published at boingboing.net, 2016), Bright Weavings
claims.quote: about the writers of history, chroniclers and artists
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'I suppose I've never looked back'

claims.claim: Kay names as a cost of his method that readers will never learn the year of the Treaty of Utrecht in his novels.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'On the Strengths of Fiction Done as Near-History' (first published at boingboing.net, 2016), Bright Weavings
claims.quote: Readers will never learn the year of the Treaty of Utrecht

claims.claim: Kay says he believes in varying the tension, drama and type of scenes in a book, and even the language the story is told in.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions', Bright Weavings, 2017
claims.quote: even the langiuage in which the story is told

claims.claim: Kay says artists are the recorders and chroniclers of a time and can become the emblems of a day for later eras.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions', Bright Weavings, 2017
claims.quote: the recorders, chroniclers of a time

claims.claim: Kay says he is interested in shaping a long view, a sense for the reader of time passing across periods.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions', Bright Weavings, 2017
claims.quote: shaping a long view, a sense for the reader of time

claims.claim: Kay says knowing the themes of history does not necessarily mean the minutiae of dates and places.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions', Bright Weavings, 2017
claims.quote: That doesn’t necessarily mean the minutiae of dates and places

claims.claim: Kay says that if a book is done well readers can be moved by a single line, because they know why the character acted.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions', Bright Weavings, 2017
claims.quote: readers can be moved by a single line

claims.claim: Kay says he is not a detached writer and is very much engaged as he writes intense or quietly moving scenes.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions', Bright Weavings, 2017

claims.claim: Kay says Children of Earth and Sky was deliberately set up to be about people who are not important in the scheme of things.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Children of Earth and Sky Author Questions', Bright Weavings, 2017
claims.quote: about people who are not important in the scheme of things

claims.claim: Kay says catching something about our own lives, even if less dramatic, is what he is always trying to do in a book.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Danica and Leonora', Bright Weavings, 2017
claims.quote: it catches something about our own lives
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'I went with my own feeling'

claims.claim: Kay reports that an experienced early reader from the book trade objected that his two women connect awfully fast.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'Danica and Leonora', Bright Weavings, 2017
claims.quote: They connect awfully fast, don’t they?
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'Here's where it got interesting'

claims.claim: Kay says he is focused on nuance and on letting readers decide what they find in or take away from a book.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Big Idea: Guy Gavriel Kay', Whatever (John Scalzi's blog), 2025
claims.quote: letting readers decide what they find in or take away

claims.claim: Kay says he is offering a story and not giving a lecture, and does not write for lessons.
claims.source: Guy Gavriel Kay, 'The Big Idea: Guy Gavriel Kay', Whatever (John Scalzi's blog), 2025
claims.quote: I’m offering a story not giving a lecture
claims.page: body, paragraph beginning 'You can write about yesterday's snows'

verdicts.trueWording: he or she cannot be sure they know where the novel they are reading is going
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'I had come to realize'; the sentence attributes it to 'this shift from following the events of history' i.e. the quarter-turn named in the same paragraph's opening line.

verdicts.trueWording: I telescoped the Reconquista in Lions. The tragedy of a culture's demise could play out in one or two generations
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the very next sentence supplies the 'one or two generations' limb, in the paragraph beginning 'It was with Lions'.

verdicts.trueWording: About Procopius the historian, about the writers of history, chroniclers and artists
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim; the paragraph beginning 'I suppose I've never looked back' names the Sarantine Mosaic as where he 'had thoughts I wanted to develop and explore that way'.

verdicts.trueWording: Readers will never learn the year of the Treaty of Utrecht in my novels
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'So, briefly told', which is explicitly introduced as 'downsides, or risks, to how I work'.

verdicts.trueWording: the need to vary the tension, drama, the type of scenes a book has, even the langiuage in which the story is told
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 4, misspelling 'langiuage' included, preceded by 'I really believe, as a writer, in what you are noting here'.

verdicts.trueWording: Artists are, more good or ill, the recorders, chroniclers of a time
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 5; the next sentence carries the second limb: 'they can become, for later eras, the emblems of a day'.

verdicts.trueWording: I am interested in shaping a long view, a sense for the reader of time passing
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 1; 'across periods' is carried by 'looking in on history at various moments and periods'.

verdicts.trueWording: That doesn't necessarily mean the minutiae of dates and places
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 2; the antecedent of 'That' is the preceding sentence's 'ignorant of the themes of history'.

verdicts.trueWording: If a book is done well, readers can be moved by a single line ... because they know why he did that
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 4; both the 'done well' condition and the 'because they know why' clause are on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: I am not a 'detached' writer ... I am very much engaged as I write them
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 4, with 'when intense things happen to my characters, or even quietly moving ones' supplying both scene types.

verdicts.trueWording: Children of Earth and Sky was deliberately set up in my mind to be about people who are not important in the scheme of things
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in answer 5; claim omits only the phrase 'in my mind'.

verdicts.trueWording: I think it catches something about our own lives, even if less dramatic, which is what I am always trying to do in a book
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'I went with my own feeling'; every limb of the claim is that one sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: one of my earliest readers, an experienced man in the book trade, expressed doubts: 'They connect awfully fast, don't they?'
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'Here's where it got interesting'; 'objected' renders the page's 'expressed doubts', and the two women are Danica and Leonora.

verdicts.trueWording: I'm focused on complicating things, multiple ideas, on nuance, on letting readers decide what they find in or take away from a book
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'Truth is'; both the nuance limb and the readers-decide limb are in the same sentence.

verdicts.trueWording: Not for lessons! I'm offering a story not giving a lecture
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim in the paragraph beginning 'You can write about yesterday's snows'; 'Not for lessons!' immediately precedes it and supports the second limb.
